title: Phase diagram of a double-occupancy cell model of a fluid with Curie-Weiss interaction
authors: R. V. Romanik, O. A. Dobush, M. P. Kozlovskii, I. V. Pylyuk, M. A. Shpot
abstract: A double-occupancy cell model of a fluid with Curie-Weiss interaction is studied. First, we show that the model is isomorphic to the Blume-Capel model on a complete graph through a simple transformation from spin to occupancy variables. We then investigate its phase behavior within the grand-canonical ensemble using a combination of analytical and numerical methods. Despite its simplicity, the model exhibits a remarkably rich thermodynamic behavior depending on the ratio between the local repulsive and global attractive interactions. We identify regimes characterized by a single critical point, two distinct critical points, tricritical behavior, and triple-point formation. For sufficiently strong repulsion, the system possesses three fluid phases of different densities, leading to both gas-liquid and liquid-liquid coexistence. The locations of the critical, tricritical, and triple points are determined, and the corresponding phase diagrams are constructed. These results demonstrate that the competition between double-occupancy repulsion and long-range attraction is sufficient to generate complex phase behavior in a minimal multiple-occupancy lattice-gas model.
summary: This paper analyzes a double-occupancy cell fluid model with Curie-Weiss interactions, demonstrating its rich phase diagram structure. By relating it to the Blume-Capel model, the authors map out multiple coexistence regimes, including gas-liquid and liquid-liquid transitions. The complexity arises from the interplay between local repulsion and global attraction.
main_problem: The study investigates the complex phase diagram and rich thermodynamic behavior of a fluid modeled by a double-occupancy cell model interacting via Curie-Weiss forces.
main_result: The competition between local repulsion and long-range attraction generates complex phase behavior, including regimes with single/double critical points, tricritical points, and triple-point formation, leading to gas-liquid and liquid-liquid coexistence.
method: The analysis uses the grand-canonical ensemble formalism, employing analytical techniques like Laplace's method on integrals derived from the partition function.
model_or_system: The system is a double-occupancy cell fluid model ($n_l \in \{0, 1, 2\}$) whose Hamiltonian is shown to be isomorphic to the Blume-Capel model on a complete graph. Interactions include global Curie-Weiss attraction and local repulsion.
key_observables: Critical temperatures ($T_c^*$), critical densities ($ho_c^*$), triple-point coordinates, and phase coexistence lines (Gas $\leftrightarrow$ LDL $\leftrightarrow$ HDL).
important_parameters: The ratio $a = \Delta/J$, which governs the transition between different types of critical points.
main_assumptions: Calculations are performed in the thermodynamic limit ($N 	o \infty$), and the analysis distinguishes results for distinguishable versus indistinguishable particles.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the phase diagrams (T*-rho* vs a) showing coexistence lines, critical point loci (blue/red), and triple-point lines (black).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the model's isomorphism, deriving the grand partition function, applying advanced mathematical techniques (Laplace's method), and then detailing the phase diagram analysis for both distinguishable and indistinguishable particle cases.
why_interesting: While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the mapping to the Blume-Capel model connects it to quantum spin systems, making the study of complex phase transitions relevant for understanding critical phenomena in many-body physics.

Red curves: the lines of critical points at a > atc. Black curve: the line of triple points in the interval atc < a < 0.5. All the lines meet at the tricritical point with a = atc = 1

Fig. 2: The T ∗−ρ∗phase diagrams of the double-occupancy cell model in the case of distinguishable particles at different values of a = ∆/J. Solid curves are the coexistence lines. (a): The coexistence line between phases I and III ends at the critical point. (b) and (c): Coexistence lines between phases I — II and II — III are present in the temperature interval T ∗ tr ≤T ∗≤T ∗ c , each ending at its own critical point. For T ∗≤T ∗ tr, phases I and III coexist. T ∗ tr is the temperature of the triple point. (d): Coexistence lines between phases I — II and II — III are present for 0 ≤T ∗≤T ∗ c , each ending at its own critical point.

Fig. 3: The phase diagram in the (T ∗, ρ∗, a)-space for the case of distinguishable particles. The figure combines representations of Figs. 1 and 2 in one view. Green dashed curves: the coexistence lines at a = 0.3, a = 0.375, a = 0.45, and a = 0.6. Blue and red curves are the critical-point lines. Black curve is the triple-point line.

Phase I: T ∗= 0.25, ρ∗= 0.1; Phase II: T ∗= 0.2, ρ∗= 0.5; Phase III: T ∗ c = 0.25, ρ∗= 1.9; Supercritical: T ∗= 0.5, ρ∗= 0.5. At r > r∗, g(2) = 1.
